newsitem.title: FRANCE: FOCUS-French markets nervous amid election concerns.
newsitem.headline: FOCUS-French markets nervous amid election concerns.

text.p: French financial markets fell on Monday amid political uncertainty ahead of an expected snap general election, seen necessary to allow the government to push through austerity measures for France to qualify for a single currency.

President Jacques Chirac launched the process of an early dissolution by meeting political leaders early in the day. In a planned national broadcast at 1800 GMT he was expected to set a general election date in late May or early June.
Chirac's move was seen as a high-risk political gamble to ensure the economic goal of adopting the euro by 1999 alongside Germany.
"Either it's a masterstroke or it will blow up in his face. If it works it will be a masterstroke, but it will be very uncertain for the next month," equities strategist Gary Dugan at JP Morgan said.
The franc, stocks, bonds and interest rate contracts all suffered from the climate of political uncertainty, extending last week's losses.

Trading on the June contract for Paris Interbank Offered Rates (PIBOR) soared to a hefty 103,166 lots and the contract settled down 19 basis points at 96.30. Non-residents were bailing out, followed by domestic investors, an analyst said.

The benchmark 10-year June French franc bond future fell 0.44 to 128.28. The yield spread -- reflecting the risk premium for holding French bonds - between the French and the underlying German bond contract narrowed to minus seven basis points from 13 a week earlier.

The franc weakened against the German currency, trading at 3.3775 per mark, compared to 3.3698 late on Friday. The French unit hit a high last week of 3.3615 against the mark, its strongest level since June 1993.
The blue-chip CAC-40 share index closed down 0.98 percent at 2,522.67. It fell 1.24 percent at the opening, after closing last Friday down 2.6 percent.

An election can be held as late as Spring 1998 but market operators believe Chirac felt he needed to act earlier, to give time to qualify in 1998 for the euro, as tougher measures will be needed to bring the public deficit to three percent of gross domestic product.
"It's pretty clear we'll see some pretty tough measures in the next few weeks," said equity salesman John Fordyce at Ferri.
But some are worried the prospect of more austerity under a centre-right government could push voters to the Socialist party.

Socialist leader Lionel Jospin on Sunday tempered his enthusiasm for a single currency when he said he would not impose tough policies to hit the three percent Maastricht deficit target if that increased unemployment - effectively setting out the election agenda.

"As long as the election result has not been announced, there is a risk," a stock market trader said. If Chirac wins a fresh mandate to maintain policies, the markets will rise. But in view of the unpopular measures, the electorate may favour the Socialists, the trader added.

Share prices have risen strongly since the start of the year, helped by a strong dollar and good fundamentals as companies reported strong profits, but that could dry up or even reverse if political risk grows in the coming weeks, JP Morgan's Dugan said.

Patrick Artus, head of financial and economic studies at the Caisse des Depots et Consignations (CDC) said, "The real reason (for the election) is that there needs to be a big increase in taxation. Spending is completely in line with forecasts, but there have been shortfalls in social security and tax payments."

Finance minister Jean Arthuis said on Monday he did not fear a market backlash from a possible early election. He told Reuters Financial Television the markets would be reassured that France had chosen the path of creating jobs through less public expenditure and lower public deficits.
